newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Risks mounting for Treasuries setback.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Risks mounting for Treasuries setback.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries have marched ahead since September but a long list of worries threatens to whittle away those gains in the months ahead, analysts said on Thursday.
With the peak Thanksgiving and Christmas buying season ready to roll, inflation could rear its ugly head. Potential yen gains pose a liquidity risk and, further out, budget wrangling looms.
These factors will put upward pressure on Treasury yields and outward pressure on the 10-year T-note/German Bund yield spread, currently at 45 basis points, analysts said.

"On a three month view, we've got the spread moving out to about 60 basis points on underformance of the U.S.," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London. "That is based on our view that if we do get strong growth early next year the market will sell off," he said.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. bond was quoted at 100-12/32 at 1300 GMT in London, giving a yield of 6.471 percent, just off an eight-month low of 6.45 percent hit on Tuesday.
Treasury prices have climbed steadily and yields dropped since September as the U.S. economy slowed from its second quarter breakneck speed and inflation remained at bay.
Many analysts say Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has carefully nutured this "Goldilocks" scenario, with the economy neither too hot, nor too cold, but just right.
The Fed's decision on Wednesday to keep interest rates on hold should allow the fairy tale to continue, some say.
But others argue that the recently restrained but powerful U.S. consumer sector is set to spring into action as Thanksgiving on November 28 and Christmas approach.
Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking, expects sales to be fairly brisk, and said that will help the T-note/Bund gap to swell to 90 basis points by early next year.

"We have had a third quarter pause in consumer spending. That has left consumers in a much more comfortable financial position from the middle of the year when they were looking overstretched and overborrowed," he said.

Chester agreed. He said economic data were likely to be supportive until the end of the year. Indeed, October consumer and retail sales numbers released on Thursday were subdued. But much of next year's interest rate policy hinges on the consumer and that will depend on holiday spending patterns.

Anaylsts said signs of a recovering yen could also begin to pose problems for Treasuries, although a recent attempt by the yen to push higher appears to have faded. T-bonds have been supported by a wall of Japanese money from investors borrowing in yen and taking advantage extremely low interest rates.

"If the yen does appreciate significantly against the dollar from here and Japanese authorities are intent on adopting a stronger yen policy, then we could see signficant outflows of Japanese capital from U.S. Treasuries," said Chester.
Further ahead, budget shenanigans could also upset Treasuries, analysts said.

While Democrat President Bill Clinton appears to have recently eased his opposition to Republican proposals for a balanced budget amendment, the road to an agreement will be strewn with political and technical obstacles, analysts said.
"That is going to be the big thing for the Treasury market in 1997," said Lewis.
Chester said the key date for the budget will come when Clinton gives his State of the Union address and outlines formal proposals. Until then, speculation will swing the market.
David Bloom, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London, is not overtly negative Treasuries but said investors should not be lulled into believing the Goldilocks story.
"There is a sense of complacency over the U.S. at the moment in that everyone is looking for a golden scenario and that Greenspan has achieved the perfect steady state," he said.
"Quite frankly from this type of levels you can get a surprise in either direction to shock the market," he said, also citing consumer spending as the possible spark.
